Description
I am recruiting one or more MS or PhD students to join my lab in the Department of Biology at the
University of North Dakota, with a target start of Summer/Fall 2027. This is a new lab so incoming
students will have real input into shaping its culture and research direction.

My research examines food web and trophic dynamics in freshwater ecosystems using diet, stable isotope
and other approaches, with particular interest in how climate change and disturbance (wildfire, shifting
thermal and hydrologic regimes) reshape lake and stream food webs. My own field experience spans
watersheds in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest, but I'm equally interested in students who want to
develop projects in North Dakota's own freshwater systems — prairie pothole lakes, the Red River, Devils
Lake — or Northern Minnesota’s boundary waters and prairie-to-boreal ecotone. Potential research
directions include, but are not limited to:
●Fish and invertebrate secondary production in streams, rivers, and lakes
●Trophic responses of lakes and streams to wildfire or other acute disturbances
●Climate-driven shifts in thermal regime and cascading effects on food webs
●Braided river channel production and food web dynamics
●Stable isotope and biomarker approaches to tracking energy flow in aquatic systems
●Comparative food web structure across gradients of hydrologic connectivity or land use

Students will be trained in traditional stream ecology, stable isotope methods, quantitative food web
analysis, field sampling design, statistical/programming approaches (R), and scientific writing, and will
be supported in attending and presenting at national conferences.

Qualifications
Required:
●B.S. in ecology, biology, environmental science, or a related field
●Genuine interest in freshwater ecosystems and willingness to develop independent research skills
●Ability to work both independently and collaboratively
●Willingness to conduct fieldwork in variable conditions
Preferred:
●Prior field or laboratory research experience
●Familiarity with R or another statistical/programming environment

Funding
Incoming students begin on a Department of Biology Teaching Assistantship, with a stipend of
roughly $1,888/month (MS) or $2,388/month (PhD), tuition waiver, and health insurance.
Transition to a Research Assistantship is anticipated pending success of pending grant proposals.

To Apply
Interested applicants should submit the following as a single PDF to [email removed] with the
email subject line “GA Position (Last Name)”:
1. A brief cover letter (1 page) describing your research interests, relevant experience, and career
goals
2. A CV or resume
3. Contact information for three references
Considering applications on a rolling basis until January 31, 2027. Formal application to the UND
Biology graduate program is a separate step, due February 15 — happy to discuss timing with any
interested applicant.
Contact
Dr. Matt Dunkle Department of Biology, University of North Dakota [email removed]

The Environmental Psychology Innovation Center (EPIC) in the Biology Department at University of Miami (Go Canes!) is recruiting a graduate student to begin January or August 2027. Description
Dr. Alison O’Dowd (https://www.humboldt.edu/environmental-science-and-management/alison-odowd) at Cal Poly Humboldt seeks applications for highly motivated students interested in pursuing graduate school in the Environmental Science & Management option of the Natural Resources Graduate Program (https://www.humboldt.edu/cnrs/graduate-programs/natural-resources). Students with an interest in estuarine invertebrates, aquatic food webs, bioenergetics models, and invertebrates as food resources for juvenile salmonids are particularly encouraged to apply.

Project Summary
The objective of this research is to understand the impact of a restoration project in the Eel River Estuary (at Cannibal Island in Northern California) on rearing habitat and landscape-scale growth potential for juvenile salmonids and other native fish species that inhabit the site. To do this, we will quantify the changes in rearing habitat (i.e., area, water quality characteristics, and invertebrate biomass availability) and potential bioenergetic differences (derived from observed differences in invertebrate biomass) for juvenile salmonids (Chinook, Coho) and other fish in the assemblage. The proposed approach is to collect pre- and post- restoration food web, water quality, and physical habitat data, stage and velocity at monthly intervals, in the restoration area and a nearby control site, during periods of key estuary rearing for juvenile salmonids (e.g. December-August). These data can be evaluated as meaningful stand-alone metrics (e.g. changes in invertebrate density and biomass, water quality and physical habitat) and integrated into a bioenergetics model to predict changes on landscape scale productivity (e.g. joules of fish growth potential per area per time). We will also explore the role of Cannibal Island as a producer and exporter of food to adjacent foraging habitat in the North Bay of the Eel River Estuary pre- and post-restoration construction. 

This graduate research project will seek to understand the invertebrate responses post-restoration to assess food resources for out-migrating juvenile salmonids and other fish. Collection and identification of estuarine invertebrates, building a bioenergetics model, and interpretation of data will be the primary tasks associated with this project.

Assistantship
·         Compensation for two years to cover living expenses and tuition ($24,000/year)
·         Project-related expenses (travel to field sites, equipment, etc.) will be covered
·         Funding to present graduate research at a professional conference

The second year of funding is conditional based on student academic standing and project progress. Program start date is August 2027.

Teaching Assistant (TA) positions with a tuition waiver may be available to qualified candidates.

Requirements
Strong applicants will have:
-          An undergraduate degree in Entomology, Zoology, Ecology, Environmental Science, Biology, Fisheries, Watershed Science, or related field
-          An undergraduate GPA of 3.0 or above
-          University-level courses in disciplines such as: ecology, fisheries, entomology, aquatic ecology, ecological restoration, and/or statistics
-          Demonstrated experience working in aquatic habitats (such as tidal sloughs, estuaries, rivers, streams, lakes) and with associated field equipment
-          Demonstrated experience sorting and identifying aquatic invertebrates
-          Demonstrated experience managing others in a laboratory setting
-          Ability to drive to field sites
-          An interest in publishing research findings in a scientific journal

To Apply:

Send a single PDF to [email removed] that includes: 

(1)    A brief letter of interest including your background and research interests.  Describe your specific experience:
a.       Conducting field work in aquatic habitats (particularly tidal sloughs or estuaries);
b.       Sorting and identification of aquatic invertebrates;
c.       Managing others in a laboratory setting; and
d.       Whether you are (or will be by August 2027) a California resident.
 (2)    A resume/CV (including undergraduate GPA)
(3)    Transcripts (unofficial is fine)
(4)    Names, emails and phone numbers for three references

The priority application deadline is November 10, 2026. Applications will be accepted on a rolling basis until a student is selected for the position. After initial screening, the candidate will be asked to submit a formal application for the fall 2027 semester through CalState apply (https://www2.calstate.edu/apply/graduate). Applications will be considered until position is filled.

Applicants from diverse backgrounds are especially encouraged to apply.

Cal Poly Humboldt is a comprehensive public university with world-class graduate programs in natural resource management, located on the North Coast of California; with access to mountains, beaches, and the largest old growth redwood forests in the world all nearby. Visit www.humboldt.edu for more information.

For more information about the Environmental Science & Management option in the Natural Resources Masters Program go to: https://www.humboldt.edu/academics/programs/natural-resources

Description
*Applications are reviewed on a rolling-basis.

ARS Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is available with the U. S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service (ARS), National Animal Disease Center (NADC), Food Safety and Enteric Pathogens Research Unit located in Ames, Iowa. Relocation will be required.

The Agricultural Research Service (ARS) is the U.S. Department of Agriculture's chief scientific in-house research agency with a mission to find solutions to agricultural problems that affect Americans every day from field to table. ARS will deliver cutting-edge, scientific tools and innovative solutions for American farmers, producers, industry, and communities to support the nourishment and well-being of all people; sustain our nation’s agroecosystems and natural resources; and ensure the economic competitiveness and excellence of our agriculture. The vision of the agency is to provide global leadership in agricultural discoveries through scientific excellence.

Research Project: This project at the Food Safety and Enteric Pathogens Research Unit is focused on identifying methods to reduce Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli in food producing animals.  Under the guidance of the mentor, the participant will be involved in conducting in vitro and/or in vivo (animals) experiments evaluating microbial colonization factors and host responses, characterizing bacteria/bacterial communities, testing dietary and other control modalities, as part of the learning experience. This will include various culture methods, nucleic acid extraction, PCR methods, sequence analysis, immunohistochemistry, cell/tissue processing, and ELISA/immunoblots, and the scientific communication of research findings.

Learning Objectives: Under the guidance of a mentor, you will have the opportunity to learn to: (a) strengthen microbiological, molecular biological, immunological and histological techniques; (b) develop lab protocols; (c) collect and analyze data with statistics

Mentor(s): The mentor for this opportunity is Indira Kudva ([email removed]). If you have questions about the nature of the research, please contact the mentor(s).

Anticipated Appointment Start Date: 2026/2027. Start date is flexible and will depend on a variety of factors.

The Department of Forestry in the College of Forest Resources and the Forest and Wildlife Research Center at Mississippi State University is seeking applicants for a funded M.S. assistantship to examine the professional readiness of forestry graduates and the competency needs of employers across public, private, and non-profit natural resource sectors. Description
The Wisely Lab in the University of Florida Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation is recruiting a Ph.D. student to join a multidisciplinary project developing innovative approaches for surveillance of feral swine and African swine fever virus (ASFV).

The project uses mosquito bloodmeals as biological samples of free-ranging feral swine, an approach known as exogenous xenosurveillance. By treating blood-fed mosquitoes as “flying syringes,” the research team will evaluate whether mosquito bloodmeals can be used to detect feral swine, genetically identify individual animals, estimate population abundance, and support pathogen surveillance.


Position responsibilities

The Ph.D. student will take a leading role in the field ecology and quantitative components of the project. Responsibilities will include:

·         Coordinating deployment and sampling of camera traps and mosquito capture systems across wet and dry seasons.

·         Supervising and mentoring undergraduate researchers participating in field and laboratory activities.

·         Working with project collaborators to process mosquito bloodmeals and generate genetic data for individual identification of feral swine.

·         Developing genetic mark-recapture models to estimate feral swine abundance from mosquito-derived host DNA.

·         AND/OR

·         Developing occupancy/detection models to compare the effectiveness of mosquito-based surveillance and conventional camera trapping.

The student will be co-advised by Dr. Samantha Wisely, a wildlife disease ecologist in UF's Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, and Dr. Nathan Burkett-Cadena, a vector-borne disease ecologist at the UF Florida Medical Entomology Laboratory. The student will also collaborate closely with Dr. Tim Smyser of the USDA APHIS Wildlife Services National Feral Swine Damage Management Program on genomic approaches for individual identification of feral swine. The student will have the opportunity to also interact with Dr. Amy Vittor from the College of Medicine on serological assay development. 

An important feature of the project is the integration of research with agricultural biosecurity education. The successful candidate will work closely with a Ph.D. student specializing in science communication/agricultural education, sharing field experiences, data and scientific expertise that will inform educational materials, microcredentials and a graduate learning module in genetic mark-recapture. The science communications Ph.D. student, mentored by Dr. Grady Roberts, will lead development of the educational products; this position will contribute scientific content and collaborate on their development but will not lead the project's education component.


Minimum qualifications

Applicants should have:

·         A bachelor's or master's degree in wildlife ecology, ecology, entomology, biology, quantitative ecology, disease ecology, or a related field.

·         Previous experience conducting ecological field research.

·         Demonstrated interest in wildlife population ecology, wildlife disease, quantitative ecology, or wildlife surveillance.

·         Experience with, or strong interest in learning, population modeling and statistical analysis in R.

·         Ability and willingness to conduct extended fieldwork under hot, humid and physically demanding Florida conditions.

·         Strong organizational, written communication and teamwork skills.

·         Ability to work independently while contributing effectively to a highly interdisciplinary research team.

Experience with camera trapping, mosquito or other arthropod sampling, molecular ecology/genetics, occupancy modeling, capture-recapture analysis, or supervision of field crews is desirable but not required.


Research environment

The student will join a collaborative team spanning wildlife disease ecology, entomology, genomics, infectious disease and agricultural education, with collaborators at the University of Florida and USDA APHIS Wildlife Services. The project provides an unusual opportunity for a doctoral student to integrate intensive field ecology with molecular tools and quantitative population modeling while conducting research with direct application to wildlife management and U.S. agricultural biosecurity. 

Location: University of Florida, Gainesville, Florida, with substantial fieldwork throughout Florida.
Degree: Ph.D. in Wildlife Ecology and Conservation
Advisor: Wisely, with co-advising by Nathan Burkett-Cadena

This USDA AFRI funded graduate assistanceship has four years of funding and would begin in May of 2027. Please send a cv and cover letter to Samantha Wisely at [email removed] by November 15, 2026.

Description
Northern Prairie Wildlife Research Center is seeking 6 -12 student contractor technicians for the 2027 summer field season for Piping Plover studies. Technicians will be placed on crews of 2-3 people and will be responsible for monitoring breeding plovers on emergent sandbars within riverine habitats along the Missouri River in the Northern Great Plains.  They will contribute to nest searching, nest monitoring, erecting predator exclosures, banding adult and chicks, resighting bands with spotting scopes, binoculars, and digital cameras and data entry in Microsoft Access/Survey123.  Students will be trained in data-collection methods at the beginning of the field season. Students will receive motorboat training.
 Field work is extensive and requires long hours walking on river sandbars and operating motorboats in adverse weather conditions. The incumbent may be required to lift containers weighing up to 40 pounds in the performance of assigned duties. Field work will involve exposure to a wide range of weather conditions including cold, mud, and severe heat.  Exposure to biting insects and ticks is possible. At the end of each field day, students are expected to enter data into databases in an office setting. Housing will be provided and may be bunkhouse setting, a field house, camper, and/or apartments.

Students must be in good academic standing and enrolled in a degree program at a recognized educational institution or be able to show proof of graduation from a recognized educational institution (diploma).
 Must be able to follow an established monitoring protocol and accurately record data.  Students may be required to take and pass the government boat operators course (MOCC) at the beginning of the field season. Applicants with a working knowledge of GPS units, nest searching, band resighting, and boat operation experience are especially encouraged to apply.

    Description
 The Avian Ecology Program at Archbold Biological Station is seeking four Post-Baccalaureate Research Fellows (PBRFs) for seasonal appointments of at least six months to assist with one of the world's longest-running studies of wild birds: a 57-year research program focused on the demography, ecology, behavior, and conservation of the federally threatened Florida Scrub-Jay (Aphelocoma coerulescens). Four positions will begin on February 1, 2027. Two appointments will continue through July 2027, while the remaining two will continue through mid-September 2027. 

 Fellows will be mentored by Dr. Sahas Barve and work within a dynamic research team that includes three research assistants. This is a seasonal position paying $15.00 per hour for approximately 29 hours per week. Because this position is classified as seasonal, traditional employee benefits are not provided at hire. Archbold determines benefit eligibility for seasonal employees using the Affordable Care Act (ACA) look-back measurement method. 

 Lodging is provided, and residence at Archbold Biological Station is required for the duration of the fellowship. 

 A unique feature of this fellowship is the opportunity to develop an independent research project, either through the collection of new field data or by leveraging Archbold's extensive long-term Florida Scrub-Jay dataset. We particularly encourage applications from individuals who are enthusiastic about pursuing independent research and gaining hands-on experience in ecological field studies, data analysis, and scientific inquiry. 

 
Requirements
Key Responsibilities 
 PBRFs contribute to several aspects of this research, but their primary duties include:  
 Independently searching for and monitoring nests  
 Conducting monthly censuses of color-banded birds 
 Daily data entry 
 Habituating birds for subsequent trapping 
 Conducting oak acorn surveys  
 Surveying FLSJ populations at other sites 
 In addition, PBRFs may assist in collecting blood samples from jays, mapping jay territories, and helping with prescribed fires  

Required Qualifications 
 Bachelor’s degree. This position is ideal for students with undergraduate degrees contemplating graduate school in the fields of Ecology, Evolution, Conservation Biology, and Natural Resource Management.  


 Experience
 Field experience outside of coursework; however, we provide all required training for all PBRFs.  
 Resighting color-banded birds 
 Finding and monitoring nests 
 Using a compass or GPS  
 Ability to navigate and work alone in the field but coordinate duties with a small team to achieve all project goals. 
 Certifications/Licenses 
 A valid US Driver’s License  
 Experience searching for nests of open-cup nesters, preferred 
 Please note that we are unable to provide international applicants with a work visa. US citizenship or permission to work legally in the US is required.


 Knowledge, Skills, and Abilities
 Attention to detail with respect to following sampling protocols and managing data 
 Tolerance for biting insects, early mornings, and high heat/humidity 
 Motivation and enthusiasm about living and working at a rural field-station 
 Respect for others, as PBRFs will share lodging with other PBRFs 
 Effective and responsive communication with supervisors, coworkers, and roommates 

 
Work Environment & Physical Requirements
 Employees must be able to perform the essential functions of their position with or without reasonable accommodation. Depending on the role, work may require sitting, standing, walking, bending, reaching, lifting and carrying materials, repetitive hand movements, and operating standard office, laboratory, field, or maintenance equipment. Some positions may involve working outdoors in varying weather conditions, traversing uneven terrain, and occasional travel. Physical requirements will vary by position and will be specified in the individual job description. 
   

 Why Join Archbold?
 Joining Archbold means becoming part of a mission-driven organization dedicated to advancing scientific research, conservation, and education. Employees have the opportunity to contribute meaningful work that supports the understanding and preservation of natural ecosystems while collaborating with passionate, talented professionals. Archbold fosters a culture of innovation, teamwork, and continuous learning, providing an environment where employees can grow professionally while making a lasting impact on science, conservation, and the communities we serve. Eligible employees also enjoy competitive compensation and benefits package designed to support their well-being and professional success.

 Complete the application here, and include the following in a single pdf titled with your surname: 
 A single-page cover letter outlining how your previous experiences and interests are relevant to the job responsibilities and qualifications listed above. Be sure to mention your research interests and describe how this position aligns with your personal experiences and goals. 
A CV
The names and contact information of three references 


For questions, please contact Hannah Miller ([email removed]). We will start reviewing applications after the deadline on October 20, 2026, and hope to finalize hires by ~1 month after this date.

 $15.00 hourly, seasonal-not benefit eligible

EPA Office/Lab and Location: A research opportunity is currently available at the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution Prevention (OCSPP), Great Lakes Coastal Environmental Science Laboratory located in Duluth, Minnesota.

The mission of EPA is to protect human health and the environment. EPA works to ensure that: Americans have clean air, land and water; National efforts to reduce environmental risks are based on the best available scientific information; Federal laws protecting human health and the environment are administered and enforced fairly, effectively and as Congress intended; Environmental stewardship is integral to U.S. policies concerning natural resources, human health, economic growth, energy, transportation, agriculture, industry, and international trade, and these factors are similarly considered in establishing environmental policy; All parts of society have access to accurate information sufficient to effectively participate in managing human health and environmental risks; Contaminated lands and toxic sites are cleaned up; and chemicals in the marketplace are reviewed for safety.

Research Project: The US EPA is mandated to address the endocrine disrupting potential of thousands of chemicals. For the majority of these chemicals there is a lack of information regarding whether they have the potential to cause adverse effects from impacts on thyroid hormone status. Understanding the important targets within the network of processes involved in maintaining normal functioning thyroid hormone levels, and what approaches to best assess activity at those targets are critical to developing a comprehensive approach to evaluating thyroid hormone disrupting potential of large numbers of chemicals.  

Recently, a number of thyroid-related in vitro high-throughput screening (HTS) assays have been developed to broaden assay coverage for molecular targets potentially leading to thyroid disruption and were implemented to screen US EPA’s ToxCast Phase 1, 2 and E1K chemical libraries. This battery of thyroid-related in vitro HTS assays can be employed to rapidly assess potential interference with these targets. However, this screening approach leaves uncertainties regarding the meaning of in vitro activity data as it relates to in vivo adverse outcomes. Part of this research effort aims to develop a translational process that integrates relevant information, models, and data streams to provide richer context to interpret in vitro results related to thyroid disruption. As part of the translational process, this research opportunity will focus on the development of a bio-assay to quantitative monitor thyroid hormone synthesis as a complimentary assay to existing in vitro thyroid-related assays. Assay development will be followed by the analysis of canonical and suspected thyroid disrupting chemicals to understand whether, or how, in vitro activity of chemicals translates to in vivo outcomes. Additionally, this research will employ existing computational tools such as the octanol-water partition coefficient (logKow) and quantitative structure-activity relationships (QSAR) models to provide deeper interpretation of in vitro data and further prioritize chemicals most likely to impact thyroid function in aquatic systems. The translational principles employed will have much broader applicability across ToxCast HTS assays and aquatic vertebrates. 

With guidance from the mentor, you may be involved in any or all of the following training activities:

Analyzing gene expression using real-time polymerase chain reaction and developing novel primers, probes, and standards for gene expression analyses.
Developing high-throughput techniques for collection, batch processing, and analysis of biofluid and tissue samples suitable for molecular, biochemical, and/or histological analyses.
Conducting aquatic toxicology experiment using flow-through exposure systems. 
Developing and evaluating exposure strategies suitable for methodologically-challenging chemicals such as highly non-polar substances (e.g., high octanol-water partitioning coefficients), volatile chemicals, reactive chemicals, etc.
Performing quality assurance and quality control of experimental data and processes. 
Processing and analyzing large, high content, data sets using both existing and novel computational pipelines.
Analyzing experimental data and generating tables, figures, and other summaries of results.
Conducting statistical analyses including the use of hypothesis testing, regression-based approaches, multi-variate statistics, concordance analyses, etc.
Presenting research results at scientific meetings and participating in written reports and journal articles.
Learning Objectives:  You will join and learn from a transdisciplinary research team engaged in multiple aspects of project planning, communication, research implementation, and analysis. You will have the opportunity to interact with internationally recognized leaders, both within and outside EPA. 

During this appointment, you will:

Learn how to participate in and/or publish original research.
Learn a breadth of laboratory, analytical, and computational techniques which can be applied across life sciences research fields.
Learn to operate and use a range of scientific equipment.
Learn to evaluate data quality, trouble shoot research results, apply statistical methods for data analysis and interpretation.

Appointment Length: The appointment will initially be for one year, and may be renewed three to four additional years upon EPA recommendation and subject to availability of funding.

Participants do not become employees of EPA, DOE or the program administrator, and there are no employment-related benefits. Proof of health insurance is required for participation in this program. Health insurance can be obtained through ORISE.

ORISE offers all ORISE EPA graduate students and Postdocs a free 5 year membership to the National Postdoctoral Association (NPA).

The successful applicant(s) will be required to comply with Environmental, Safety and Health (ES&H) requirements of the hosting facility.

Qualifications

Candidates with a bachelor's degree may be considered if they can demonstrate strong laboratory experience. Degree must have been received within the past 5 years.

Preferred Skills:

You will also help with field testing at partner facilities, gather feedback from stakeholders, and support the creation of clear guidance and training materials. You will also have opportunities to explore a wide range of conservation and applied research projects at USDA Forest Service Pacific Southwest Research Station’s Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry, including work in forest health, invasive species, ecosystem restoration, and native habitat conservation across Hawai‘i and the Pacific.
